pages.text: Kill the anomaly, spare the normal. $(thing)CRISPR$() cuts DNA where a guide RNA matches, so it can write a trigger only the anomalous genome will read - restoring $(thing)apoptosis$(), the death a damaged cell was always meant to accept. $(thing)CAR-T$() cells are a patient's own T cells given a receptor for the anomaly's marker: living drugs that multiply as they find their target.

And dose: n fractions of D let each cell survive with probability e^{−αD−βD²}. The anomaly is resolved only if not one of its N₀ clonogens survives: TCP = exp(−N₀e^{−n(αD+βD²)}). Normal tissue repairs between fractions; its damage grows as BED = nD(1 + D/3) - so many small fractions beat a few large ones.

Build the $(item)Anomaly Resolution Engine$(). Its console is that trade: TCP above one half, normal-tissue BED below 120 Gy. The $(item)Gene Sequencer$() writes $(item)Apoptosis Triggers$(); the $(item)Bioreactor$() engineers $(item)CAR-T Cell Culture$(). In the Engine, a resistant clone with a trigger and CAR-T cells goes into remission: sixteen ordinary stem cells again, and $(fluid)Renormalised Essence$().
A CRISPR-written instruction that only an anomalous cell will read: a reminder of the death it was always supposed to accept.$(br2)Made in $(item)Gene Sequencer$().
Killer T cells taught a new receptor: they hunt one marker, the anomaly's own, and they multiply as they find it.$(br2)Made in $(item)Bioreactor$().
